source_group: Modern field surveys of Adivasi astronomy
summary_findings: Five modern field surveys, covering eleven communities that the printed record of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries does not reach at all. tribal.json was built from colonial lexicography and ethnography and could name only five communities with a sky nomenclature deep enough to call a system; this file adds the Banjara, the Kolam, the Korku, three Nicobar island communities and the Bhil, Mavchi Bhil, Vasave Bhil, Pawra and Kokna, all recorded between 2013 and 2023 by teams working village by village with a questionnaire. Every one of these papers is in copyright, so every entry here is paraphrased and every `quote` is null, on the footing tribal.json already established for its twenty Gondi entries. THE FOUR THREADS tribal.json IDENTIFIED ALL HOLD, AND ONE OF THEM GETS SHARPER. (1) THE COT: the Big Dipper is a cot in Kolami (Mandater), a cot of the DEAD in Lambadi (Jamakhat, from Yama), a hen-basket on Chowra (Lonob) and a COFFIN on Teressa (Rohiung), and the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna all have the cot with its leg pulled crooked by a thief. Lambadi is Indo-Aryan, Kolami and Bhili are Dravidian and Indo-Aryan respectively, Korku is Munda, Nicobarese is island Austroasiatic — and the death sense, which tribal.json found only in Mundari's bier, now appears three times in unrelated languages. (2) THE THIEVES: three of them, everywhere, but WHO they are is local. Korku numbers them (Pahila, Dusara, Tisara chor); the Kolams make them a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan; the Bhils make them the village elder, the chief, the sheriff and the revenue collector. The figure is shared, the cast is politics. (3) ORION IS AN IMPLEMENT, NOT A HUNTER: a seed drill for the Kolams (Tipan) and the Bhils (Pambar), a full plough with two bullocks and a ploughman for the Korku (Harnangar, Doba 1, Doba 2, Nangarnara manus). The single exception is the Banjaras, a trading people, who keep the mainstream deer (Halni) and, the paper notes, barely look at Orion otherwise. (4) THE MILKY WAY IS A ROAD WITH ANIMALS ON IT: Kolam Margam 'an animal path', Banjara Mardaar wat 'the path of the dead or of animals', Bhil and Mavchi 'the path of cows'. The Nicobarese are the exception the earlier file already predicted: on Camorta and Teressa it is a spring of water. THE BIRD AND ITS EGGS, which tribal.json called a subtler fourth thread, turns out to be the most productive figure of all. Kolam Kovela Kor is the Pleiades as one large bird and several small ones, Kolam Bhori is Aldebaran the bird with two eggs, Korku Pankheru is Sirius the bird with Bhori Aakom its eggs — the same word Bhori in a Dravidian and a Munda language — and among the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna a single bird named hulgi carries Orion's Belt, the Pleiades and a triangle of Auriga as its eggs in different villages. The figure is stable; the stars it lands on are not. TWO OTHER RESULTS. Kolam Irukmara, the Mahua tree at Crux with an old woman and a young woman gathering its flowers beneath it, is almost certainly the same word as Gondi Irukna Mara, which tribal.json had to record as unidentified for want of a modern equivalent; this file does not alter that entry but the two should be read together. And the Bhil Milky Way at Varpada is a kinship rule drawn on the sky: the band forks because a woman meeting her husband's elder brother on the road must turn aside, and the avoidance is a real rule of conduct in these communities. NEGATIVE AND UNOBTAINED. No name is claimed for the pole star among the Banjaras, who identify it but did not name it to the recorders; none for the Korku words for comet and meteor, which the paper describes ('a broom star', 'stellar excreta') without printing; and none for the Korku Lupus figure, for which only the English gloss 'Tree of Mahua' is given. The second-hand Nicobarese lists quoted inside the 2018 paper from Rajamanickam (1997) and Justine (2013) — Onchiana for Centaurus, Thyan for Orion, Mahayuvan for Crux, Musaha for Ursa Major, Gna-gna-hyaam for the Pleiades, and Justine's Chowra and Kondule constellation lists — are NOT entered: they are transcriptions at second hand, and this database does not rest an entry on those. They are the obvious next thing to chase. Three further papers of the same programme were not obtained and no entry is offered from them: the Pardhi study, the Cholanaikkan study, and the Warli, Dhodia, Katkari and Kokna study.

THE COT AGAIN, AND EXPLICITLY A DEATH-COT. tribal.json identified the cot as the one figure shared across unrelated families (Santali buḍhi parkom ipil, Kurukh khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō, Gondi Sedona Katul, Chhattisgarhi Dhuri); Mundari alone turned it into a bier. caveats: EVERY SOURCE IN THIS FILE IS IN COPYRIGHT AND NOTHING IS QUOTED. All five papers date from 2013-2023. The findings are paraphrased, the page is cited, `quote` and `quote_lang` are null throughout, and the wording of the glosses is the recorders' own only where a gloss is a single word or a fixed phrase for which no paraphrase is possible. This is the convention tribal.json set for its Gondi entries and it is followed here without exception.

The Greek letters are unrecoverable from the Korku paper. The ADS scan of JAHH 19(2) renders every Greek glyph as a solid black box — in the page image, not merely in the extracted text — so 'Rigil Kent (α Cen)' reads as 'Rigil Kent ( Cen)'. Where the paper also prints the star's proper name the Bayer letter is unambiguous and has been restored (Alioth = ε UMa, Alnitak = ζ Ori, and so on). Where it prints only the lost letter and a constellation, nothing is restored: Bharada and Patni are graded 'unidentified', Pati 'unidentified' with its magnitude also garbled in the source, and Miryan 'likely' on a magnitude-and-position argument that is stated in its notes and not written into modern_star.

The Bhil paper could not be read as text at all. Its embedded font subsets carry no ToUnicode map, so extraction yields a monoalphabetic substitution cipher — and a different cipher per font, so the running heads, the body and the table captions each scramble differently. Every Bhil, Pawra, Mavchi, Vasave and Kokna reading in this file was read off a rendered page image at 150 dpi. Nothing was decoded by solving the cipher, because a cipher solved against English prose is not evidence for the spelling of a Bhili word.

Four entries carry no vernacular name and are kept anyway: the Kolam identification of the three trailing stars as a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan; the Bhil cot; the Mavchi Bhil Pleiades as girls crushing grain; and the Bhil Milky Way as the road of Jeth and the daughter-in-law. In each the paper reports the figure in detail but prints no vernacular word for it. The precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json. An identification without a name is a weaker record than a name with an identification, and the `name_roman` field says so in plain words rather than carrying an invented form.

Village counts are reported where the papers give them, because they are the best measure of how firmly held a figure is: the Korku cot and thieves are in all twelve villages surveyed, Kolam Kovela Kor in all ten, Banjara Jamakhat in all six, while Banjara Kamedi, Kolam Sappa and Kolam Danedare Pila rest on one or two villages each and are graded accordingly. A name from one village is not the same kind of fact as a name from twelve.

The `region` field gives the district or island where the fieldwork was done, not a claim about the whole speech community. These surveys sampled particular villages, and the papers themselves show the same community differing village by village — the Kokna call the Pleiades a heap of hay in one village and a long-tailed bird in another.

iso639_3 codes are assigned by the compiler from the community name the papers use, and the papers do not give codes. Lambadi (lmn), Kolami (kfb), Korku (kfq), Bhili (bhb), Mavchi (mvf), Vasavi (vas) and Kukna (kex) are straightforward. Two are less so: 'Pawra' is taken as Pauri Bareli (bfb), and the three Nicobar localities are assigned Central Nicobarese (ncb) for Camorta, Chaura (crv) for Chowra and Teressa (tef) for Teressa on the basis of the island named. Where a reader disagrees, the region field carries the fact and the code does not.

Cross-references in the notes to tribal.json name the parallel and do not merge the entries. Kolam Irukmara and Gondi Irukna Mara are almost certainly the same word, and this file identifies it as Crux; the Gondi entry keeps its 'unidentified' grade, because one community's identification of a cognate is evidence about the other and not proof. The same restraint applies to Banjara Medi, Kolam Met and Korku Miryan, three threshing-pole names on three different stars.

The register is `tribal` for every entry except two: Banjara Chanda for the Moon and Korku Dhur tara for the pole star, both tagged `sanskritic` because the recorders themselves flag them as close to the Sanskrit. That is their judgement, not the compiler's, exactly as with the four sanskritic tags in tribal.json.
